text: According to F.D. Davis, the acceptance of new technological systems – such as an AI-supported learningmodule—depends on "perceived usefulness" and "perceived ease of use."[9] Davis emphasizes that these twovariables must align: a system must be both sufficiently useful and easy to use to ensure acceptance andeffective utilization. Jean Piaget, a renowned psychologist, argues that "learning is an active, context-basedprocess in which new knowledge is constructed on the foundation of prior experiences."[10]Guided by Davis’ and Piaget’s frameworks, my methodology aims to ensure that the proposed AI platform isboth effective and user-friendly. By combining these theoretical insights with practical feedback from teachersand students, I seek to design a system that aligns with real-world educational needs

text: Since the year 2000, the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) has evaluated the reading,writing, and scientific understanding of 15-year-olds worldwide. However, as shown in the graphic below 1.1 ,the results of the PISA study indicate a clear downward trend in performance. In Germany, one of the keyreasons behind this decline is a growing shortage of teaching personnel. By 2030, it is estimated that 115,000to 175,000 teaching positions in Germany could remain unfilled.[1] This alarming situation demands urgentsolutions - But artificial intelligence could help to overcome this obstacle.

text: While there is already extensive literature on the use of AI in education, much of it focuses on higher education.This leaves a gap in understanding how AI can be effectively implemented in school settings, particularly toaddress foundational skills like mathematics.The central question I aim to explore is: How can AI benefit both students and teachers in improvingmathematical skills? To answer this, several related questions emerge:• How receptive are students to AI-assisted, individualized learning sessions?• In what ways can AI support teachers in evaluating students’ current levels of understanding?• How effective are AI tools in identifying and addressing specific weaknesses in mathematical skills?• What are the ethical considerations when using AI in personalized learning environments?• How do students’ attitudes and engagement with AI-assisted tools influence their overall learningoutcomes?

text: While Juji and Microsoft Azure OpenAI offer promising features, both have strength and weaknesses - be it thecomplexity of configuration and therefore the required technical expertise in Azure’s case, or the limitation ofcustomization in Juji’s case. Both also have ethical and data protection obstacles that need to be addressed.Possible difficulties include the risk of selecting participants with a strong reluctance toward AI. Recent surveysindicate that while most teachers perceive AI as potentially helpful tools, approximately 15% still view AI asdestructive. Students, on the other hand, appear less concerned about the use of AI, with only about 10%considering it potentially harmful.[11]This is an issue that needs to be addressed with the test group. What are their attitudes towards AI, and whatconcerns do they have? To address this, a short questionnaire integrated into the AI system at the beginningis essential to identify and address any acceptance barriers. If such barriers are encountered, they must beresolved before participants can fully engage with the system.Another challenge is the limited time frame. A three-week testing phase provides only a brief snapshot of thesystem’s acceptance and effectiveness. A more in-depth testing period over several months would yield clearerand more precise insights. This should be considered as a follow-up, especially if this study indicates that thetools are likely to be accepted and perceived as usefull.
